utterances.text: You didn't answer my question. Please. If this Court -- if this Court establishes command responsibility, and it seems that you'd really like that because in that way you could seek the revision of your trial in Germany?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if it were so, that would be good. But, anyway, I've just about already served half of the time, so I could serve -- you know, I'll find some way of serving the other half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And my last question: When did you admit to Mr. Tuta that you had committed the murder, and when did he hear that you had done that for the first time?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- for me, it was not a murder. And, secondly, I told him on the day when we were together with the German authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And it was the first time that he heard about it, and then he told you, in view of your confession, to surrender to the German police; is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that it? This is my final question. And, please, for the sake of truth, is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First he told me in June that I should turn me in to the German authorities. Then we send them a fax in which I said when and exactly where I would arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And the very moment when Tuta learned what you had done, this reaction came; that is, he immediately said that you should turn yourself in to the German authorities, is it?

utterances.speaker: RALF RUDIGER MRACHACZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I do not have any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness, for giving the evidence. Our special thanks will go to the German interpreters, both in this courtroom and in the booths. Without your assistance, it is impossible for us to hear this witness. We are also very grateful to the authorities in Germany for their assistance and cooperation. Witness, you may leave now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, would you please refresh our recollections concerning the tendering of the documents at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In terms of this witness or -- I think with this witness, we tendered all the -- there were only several. My apologies. We tendered -- it's been tendered before, I think, through the witness Van Hecke, but just so the record is clear, we continued to use with a number of the witnesses, and it has been tendered and, if necessary, tendered again. One was Prosecution Exhibit P704, which is the so-called roster of the Convicts' Battalion. That has been used with a number of witnesses. We have also tendered -- my apologies. I haven't written this down separately on a piece of paper. There was Exhibit 26.9, which was the photograph of the Tobacco Factory, and this witness circled the building where Tuta's headquarters was located. There was the Exhibit 26.11, which was the Park Hotel, where this witness testified he was accommodated. Just a couple more. I can do this. There was Exhibit P40, which is the photograph of Cikota, which I think has already been admitted as part of Exhibits 1 to 53. But if there's any question about that, Exhibit P40 was a photograph of Cikota. Exhibit P36 is a photograph taken at Cikota's funeral and a part of an article that was with that. The witness testified that he saw Tuta, Praljak, Andabak and others in that photograph. And I believe the others were the two photographs concerning Tuta's villa, which were Exhibits 25.5 and 25.6, which again have been previously admitted. But if there's any doubt, we tender those. I believe that's it, Your Honour. Thank you. THE COURT: Thank you. The Exhibits P1 to P53 have already been admitted into evidence. How about the Document P704, is there any objection from the Defence side?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is an objection, and what an objection. I think it is simply inconceivable to think that such evidence can be admitted into evidence of such a universal court, because the origin of these documents is unknown. All we know is they were snatched by force. We have been objecting as of day one. You have given us the deadline by which we have to explain it all, and we shall do it. I won't go into it now. We still have some days left of those 30 days. And we shall explain very clearly why we are objecting to the admission of all the documents, not only P704, but why we're objecting to the admission of all the documents that were snatched by force from the Tobacco Station where they could have, indeed, been planted by whoever or tampered with by whoever. We just looked at 704. It's not only the signature and seal are missing, and yet this is a payroll list, so how can you pay any salary without a seal, without a signature, and then produce it as evidence? So we are objecting to it, but we shall write about this all in our written submission regarding our objections within the 30-day period that was given us. Now, Your Honours, if there are no other questions regarding this, I should like to touch upon a completely different topic, with your leave, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am very sorry to have to tax your patience with these facts, but I think they become very important. An appointment with the dentist has not been made to this day, and he is really suffering. He is in very severe pain. Now he'll get angry with me, because I'm saying this. He does not want to obstruct the proceedings of this Court, but he simply cannot endure this pain. He cannot endure these whole day sessions. And we have already prepared a request -- we have filed it, and I believe you will receive it tomorrow -- not to work Wednesday afternoons, just as we are not working Friday afternoons, because he simply cannot manage these long sessions. Today when I talked to him, he said please don't do anything, let the proceedings take their course, but I think it should be done. We wrote it down, we filed it, and I believe Your Honours will receive our submission tomorrow morning. I really fail to understand, especially as you told me that he enjoy a better treatment than you and I, but it has been a fortnight, and he still hasn't an appointment -- his appointment with the dentist has not been made. I really feel embarrassed to have to ask you about this, for your intervention, but I do not know who else to turn any more. That is one thing. And finally, you see, it is 5.00 now, Your Honours. I really do not know how shall I be able to prepare myself for the cross-examination tomorrow. We have another witness, five hours were envisaged for him, for the direct examination. I really do not see how the Defence will be able to prepare for that witness. I believe I have to inform the Court for all these matters, and I apologise for taking your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, -- to bring to our attention your client's problem with his tooth. I think that's the problem of the well-organised society; that is, everything will go according to appointment. This Trial Chamber will instruct the registrar to do her best to arrange those appointments.
